name: IGF-1 LR3
route: Injection in research and gray-market use
status: Never approved for human use; sold as a research chemical and black-market product; banned in sport by WADA
mechanism: An engineered IGF-1 with an arginine swap at position 3 and an extended front end, so it binds IGF-binding proteins poorly and stays active longer

article.summary: IGF-1 LR3 is an engineered, longer-acting form of insulin-like growth factor 1 sold for muscle growth. It was never approved for people, can lower blood sugar in animals, and is banned in sport.
article.takeaway: IGF-1 LR3 is an engineered version of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) that binds IGF-binding proteins poorly, so more of it stays active. Versions of it are made for laboratory research, it has never been approved for people, and it appears on the black market for bodybuilding.[^1][^2] In animals, variants like it lowered blood sugar more strongly and for longer than IGF-1,[^3] and in people higher natural IGF-1 levels are linked to some cancers.[^4] WADA bans it, and one black-market vial was found to contain a laboratory form carrying an extra purification tag whose effects in humans are unknown.[^1][^5]
glance: Injection in gray-market use; no approved dosing
Cell and animal studies; no human trials found[^3]
Prohibited at all times (WADA lists IGF-1 and its analogues)[^5]

blocks.text: IGF-1 drives growth in muscle, bone and other tissues, but in blood most of it is held by IGF-binding proteins, which limit how much is active. LR3 combines two changes: an arginine in place of the natural amino acid at position 3, and a longer front end. Both reduce binding to those proteins, which is why the analog is more potent and longer lasting than IGF-1 in animal tests.[^3]

The evidence is from animals and cell work. In pigs, LR3 lowered blood glucose about 2- to 3-fold more potently than IGF-1 and kept it low for much longer.[^3] The searches for this entry found no human trial of LR3 for muscle growth or any other use.
The IGF-1 medicine approved for people is mecasermin, used for a rare growth disorder. See [mecasermin](/peptides/mecasermin).

items: **Low blood sugar:** variants that bind poorly to binding proteins suppressed glucose over a much longer period than IGF-1 in animals[^3]
**Cancer questions:** higher circulating IGF-1 is linked to higher risk of prostate and premenopausal breast cancer in pooled studies; whether an analog carries the same risk is unknown[^4]

**Quality:** an injection vial from the black market was found to contain a laboratory form of LR3 with a His-tag attached, whose effects in humans have not been described[^1]; analyses of black-market products also found many oxidized, lower-quality peptide forms[^2]
**No human safety or dosing data** exist

blocks.text: LR3 has never been approved for human use. WADA prohibits IGF-1 and its analogues at all times,[^5] and anti-doping laboratories have validated methods to detect it.[^2] It does not appear in any category of the FDA's May 2026 list of bulk substances nominated for pharmacy compounding.[^6]

IGF-1 LR3 is a laboratory tool with strong effects in cells and animals. It has no human trials, a known tendency to lower blood sugar in animals, an unsettled cancer question and unreliable black-market supply. Athletes subject to testing should treat it as banned.

evidence.label: Preclinical: cell and animal studies only
evidence.text: The evidence is cell culture and animal work.[^3] No human trial of the compound was found.

faq.q: Is IGF-1 LR3 the same as IGF-1 DES?
faq.a: No. Both are engineered IGF-1 variants that bind IGF-binding proteins poorly, but they differ in structure. See [IGF-1 DES](/peptides/igf-1-des).
No. It is produced for laboratory use and has never been approved for human use, though it is sold to bodybuilders.[^1][^2]
Yes. WADA prohibits IGF-1 and its analogues at all times.[^5]
